claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles is governed by suppression of precursor mobility during formation.
Rapid heating at a rate greater than 10^3 K/s followed by immediate quenching suppresses rearrangement of the metal species.
Rapid heating causes all metal species to nucleate nearly simultaneously.
Suppressing rearrangement produces a homogeneous, single-phase alloy rather than phase-separated products.
The starting material can be an intimately mixed solid or solution containing Pt, Pd, Ir, Au, and Rh precursors with limited initial atomic mobility.
An ultrafast microfluidic thermal process under inert atmosphere can deliver the proposed rapid temperature burst and immediate quench.
Rapid ramping and quenching lock in the initially mixed state by leaving insufficient time for elemental diffusion and segregation.
Immediate quenching prevents atomic diffusion that would otherwise lead to phase separation or elemental segregation.
Kinetic control is critical for stabilizing the HEA configuration.
Compared with slow heating, ultrafast processing will produce more uniformly alloyed nanoparticles.
Ultrafast processing will produce nanoparticles with high surface-atom exposure.
Ultrafast processing will avoid uncontrolled nanoparticle morphology.
Slow ramp heating permits sequential reduction and sufficient atomic mobility and therefore typically produces phase-separated or segregated multimetallic nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble metal precursor systems with similar chemical characteristics and mixing enthalpies when kinetics dominate over thermodynamics.
The mechanism may fail for systems with strong intermetallic ordering tendencies.
Large chemical differences between precursors may allow phase separation despite rapid processing.
A large surface-to-bulk atom ratio is important for efficient catalyst utilization, and nanoparticles provide such high dispersion.
The cost-effective large-scale scalability of the proposed microfluidic process is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that thermal processing rate is the only difference, but the comparison bundles heating rate, cooling/quench history, and potentially reactor platform (microfluidic versus conventional), so it is not a clean single-variable comparison.
The hypothesis labels >10^3 K/s as a high temperature even though K/s is a heating-rate unit, leaving the actual peak temperature undefined.
